messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Carlos, a 25-year-old North American man who worked as a housekeeper in a downtown hotel, came to treatment after months of feeling increasingly unable to keep his life ordered around shifts that started before dawn and ended late at night. He had grown up with a caregiver whose abuse was unpredictable and humiliating, and the memories that now tormented him were tied to a childhood night when he had been awakened in the dark, pinned by the frightening feel of a rough fabric against his skin, while a child’s crying from the next room made the whole house seem alive with threat. In the present, the same sorts of moments could seize him without warning: when he woke in his apartment before sunrise and the room was still black, when his hand brushed a particular coarse hotel towel, or when he heard children crying in the hallway outside the lobby or in the courtyard behind the building. Carlos had come to believe that other people could somehow see what had happened to him just by looking at him, and that belief made those moments feel exposing and dangerous; if he seemed marked, he reasoned, it was safer not to let anyone get too close.

At those times, the old scenes returned with overwhelming force. He described them as a film that played over and over, and when the memory came back it did not feel like a recollection but like the event itself, complete across sight, sound, touch, and the sickening sensation in his body. The feeling would hit so hard that he had to stop whatever he was doing, sometimes standing frozen in a supply closet or at the end of a hallway until he could catch his breath. Those episodes often arrived after a trigger, but they also made the triggers sharper: once the memory took over, nighttime felt more menacing, the texture of certain linens became intolerable, and a child crying nearby could instantly pull him back into the old fear. He became superalert in the hotel, scanning corridors and listening for sounds that reminded him of the past, and the more he watched for danger, the more he noticed the very cues that set him off.

Carlos’s attempts to stay safe began to organize his life around avoidance. When the dark of night or waking in darkness brought on the memories, he would drop responsibilities he knew mattered, volunteering to switch shifts, skipping errands, or putting off bills and calls so he would not have to move alone through the building before daylight. In the evenings he would drift off into a world of his own, staring at his phone or losing himself in imagined scenes until hours passed, and he made a point of never being alone with another person, preferring to stay near coworkers, houseguests, or anyone else in sight. Those strategies brought brief relief, but they also kept the traumatic material close. The more he organized his days around escape and safety, the more time he spent quietly turning the event over in his mind, and the memory stayed primed to return with the same unbearable vividness. He noticed too that these habits seemed to confirm the worst things he believed about himself: that he was not really a person to others, but something damaged and exposed, someone who had to hide because if people got a clear look they would know.

Over time, the fear of harm hardened into a general rule about people. Carlos came to feel that you could never know who would hurt you, and that conviction kept him watching everyone around him with suspicion. In the hotel, a child crying in a hallway could tighten his chest and make his skin crawl; in his apartment, a dark room at 3 a.m. could have him wide awake and listening for footsteps; a rough towel in housekeeping could stop him cold long enough for the memory to rush back. Each episode made him pull further away, and each act of withdrawing seemed to leave him more convinced that danger was everywhere and that he was somehow already singled out. By the time he sought help, he was exhausted by the constant guard he kept over himself, troubled that his work was suffering because he avoided tasks and lingered in distraction, and frightened that the cycle would never loosen. What finally brought him in was the realization that he could not keep building his life around darkness, textures, and crying children without losing more of it, and he hoped, more than anything, to feel like a person again rather than an object waiting for harm.
